titre: A Five-Day Crisis, Emergency Powers of Five Months
accroche: In 1961, a military putsch collapses in five days in Algiers: the full powers de Gaulle then assumes stay in force five months longer.
contenu_vulgarise:
## A Putsch That Quickly Collapses

In the night of April 21 to 22, 1961, four generals who had left active service (Maurice Challe, Edmond Jouhaud, Raoul Salan, and André Zeller) seize control of Algiers to prevent the independence of Algeria, which Charles de Gaulle's government is now negotiating. The hoped-for support from the rest of the army does not come: by April 25, the putsch is in disarray, and the next day General Challe surrenders.

## A Two-Stage Procedure

On April 22, de Gaulle consults the Constitutional Council, as Article 16 of the French Constitution of 1958 requires before any recourse to emergency powers. In its decision of April 23, 1961, the Council finds that the conditions laid down by that article (a serious and immediate threat to the institutions of the Republic, preventing the regular functioning of the public authorities) are met. De Gaulle invokes Article 16 that same April 23 and thus assumes, for the first and only time under the Fifth Republic, the exceptional powers this article allows him: taking the measures required by the circumstances, including in the domain of the law.

## The Gap No One Had Foreseen

Article 16 of the French Constitution of 1958 then provides no time limit and no periodic review: the president alone decides when the circumstances that justified it have ceased. De Gaulle lifts the state of exception only on September 29, 1961: one hundred fifty-nine days after proclaiming it, for a military rebellion crushed in less than a week. Throughout this interval, he acts by decisions, without Parliament, which nonetheless meets as of right while Article 16 is in force, having to consent.

The lack of safeguards does not stop at duration. By a decision of April 27, 1961 taken under Article 16, de Gaulle creates a Haut Tribunal militaire (High Military Court), an exceptional jurisdiction charged first with trying the generals of the putsch. Hearing challenges to decisions taken on that basis, the Conseil d'État rules on March 2, 1962, sitting as the Assembly for judicial matters, in the Rubin de Servens decision: the decision to resort to Article 16 “has the character of an act of government, the legality of which the Conseil d'État has no authority to assess, nor the duration of its application to review.” The measures taken in the domain that the Constitution reserves to the law have, for their part, the force of law, and are therefore equally beyond the competence of the administrative judge.

The episode remains to date the only application of Article 16, and the length of that application is criticized. The constitutional revision of July 23, 2008 adds, nearly half a century later, a review: after thirty days of exercise of the exceptional powers, the Constitutional Council can be asked to verify whether the article's conditions remain met, and it takes up the matter itself after sixty days. Its opinion remains, however, non-binding.

repere.texte: The sole use of Article 16 of the Constitution lasts five months: opened on April 23, 1961 by a decision of the Constitutional Council finding that its conditions are met, the state of exception is lifted by the President of the Republic only on the following September 29.
repere.source: Wikipedia, “Article 16 of the Constitution of the French Fifth Republic”

carte.punch: The putsch lasts five days; the full powers it triggers last five months longer.
carte.idee: In April 1961, a military putsch in Algiers collapses within days. De Gaulle, who activated Article 16 of the Constitution on the third day of the crisis, gives up the exceptional powers only five months later, on September 29, with no time limit constraining him at the time.

quiz.question: Why does the use of Article 16 in 1961 remain criticized, even though the Constitutional Council had validated its activation?
choix: Because the Constitutional Council had in fact been wrong about the seriousness of the military putsch
Because de Gaulle kept the exceptional powers for five months for a rebellion crushed in five days
Because de Gaulle had activated Article 16 without consulting the Constitutional Council
Because the French Parliament had been entirely dissolved throughout this period
quiz.explication: Nothing in Article 16 of 1958 limited the duration of the exceptional powers or provided for periodic review: the constitutional revision of 2008 added, nearly half a century later, a referral to the Constitutional Council after thirty days (its opinion remains non-binding).

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who are the four generals behind the Algiers putsch of April 1961?
choix: Massu, Salan, Challe, and de Gaulle
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text names precisely Maurice Challe, Edmond Jouhaud, Raoul Salan, and André Zeller as the four generals who had left active service and were behind the putsch.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Conseil d'État decide in the Rubin de Servens decision of March 2, 1962?
choix: That the recourse to Article 16 was unlawful and had to be annulled
That the president had to consult Parliament before any extension
That the duration of the state of exception had to be limited to thirty days
That the recourse to Article 16 is an act of government beyond its review
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text quotes the decision: the decision to resort to Article 16 has the character of an act of government whose legality and duration the Conseil d'État does not review.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the constitutional revision of July 23, 2008 change in Article 16?
choix: It simply abolishes Article 16 of the Constitution
It allows the Constitutional Council to be asked to review after thirty days of exceptional powers
It transfers the power to trigger Article 16 to the Prime Minister
It limits Article 16 to external military threats alone
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that since 2008, the Constitutional Council can be asked to review after thirty days, and must rule on its own after sixty days of exercise of the exceptional powers.
